Carry out and interpret Benedict's, iodine tests
Describe dietary fibre and the role of carbohydrate in the diet

blocks.title: Classification
blocks.md: **Monosaccharides** (single sugars): glucose, fructose, galactose. **Disaccharides** (two units joined by a **glycosidic bond**, losing water): **sucrose** = glucose + fructose; **lactose** = glucose + galactose; **maltose** = glucose + glucose. **Polysaccharides**: **starch** (energy store in plants; amylose and amylopectin), **glycogen** (energy store in animals), **cellulose** (plant cell walls; fibre).

blocks.title: Food tests
blocks.md: **Benedict's test** for **reducing sugars** (glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose): heat with Benedict's solution; blue turns green, yellow, orange, then brick-red as the amount increases. **Sucrose is non-reducing**: it gives no change until boiled with dilute acid (to hydrolyse it) and neutralised. **Iodine test** for starch: iodine solution turns blue-black.

blocks.caption: A table with the three carbohydrate groups and examples.
blocks.alt: Table: monosaccharides glucose and fructose, disaccharides sucrose and lactose, polysaccharides starch and cellulose.

blocks.title: Nutrition
blocks.md: Digestible carbohydrate gives energy (17 kJ/g in this course). Starchy staple foods also supply protein, vitamins and minerals in smaller amounts. **Dietary fibre** (non-starch polysaccharides such as cellulose and pectin) is not digested but adds bulk, helps bowel function and may reduce the risk of some diseases. High intakes of added sugar contribute to dental decay and excess energy.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'Reducing' does not mean the sugar is reduced in size: it can reduce Benedict's copper(II) ions.
- Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, not glucose and glucose.
- A negative Benedict's test does not prove the absence of sucrose.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Tests
blocks.statement: A food extract gives no colour change with Benedict's solution, but gives a brick-red colour after boiling with dilute acid and neutralising. What does it contain?
steps: No change at first: no reducing sugar present.
After acid hydrolysis it gives a reducing sugar: the extract contains sucrose (a non-reducing sugar).

blocks.title: Example 2 - Starch
blocks.statement: Name the test and result for starch in a boiled yam extract.
steps: Add a few drops of iodine solution.
A blue-black colour shows starch is present.

objectives: Describe a triglyceride and its formation
Distinguish saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids
Describe essential fatty acids and cholesterol in outline
Explain the roles of fat in the diet and in food
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Palm-oil saturated-fat statement is general; check local composition tables. Cholesterol statements simplified.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Structure
blocks.md: A **triglyceride** is one **glycerol** joined to three **fatty acids** by **ester bonds**; three water molecules are released (condensation). Fatty acids differ in chain length and in **double bonds**: **saturated** (no C=C double bonds), **monounsaturated** (one) and **polyunsaturated** (more than one). More double bonds make a fat softer or liquid at room temperature.

blocks.title: Sources and roles
blocks.md: Animal fats (butter, fat on meat) contain more saturated fat; vegetable oils and fish oils contain more unsaturated fat; **palm oil** contains a fairly high proportion of saturated fat. Fat gives concentrated energy (37 kJ/g), carries fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), provides **essential fatty acids**, insulates, protects organs, and adds flavour and texture to food.

blocks.caption: Glycerol joined to three fatty acid chains.
blocks.alt: Triglyceride diagram: one glycerol joined to three fatty acids.

blocks.title: Cholesterol and health
blocks.md: **Cholesterol** is a lipid made by the body and also found in animal foods. Diets high in saturated fat are associated with higher blood cholesterol and a higher risk of heart disease; replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat is a common recommendation. **Trans fatty acids** (from partial hydrogenation) are advised to be minimised.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'Oil' and 'fat' are chemically the same class; the difference is the physical state.
- Vegetable does not mean low in saturated fat: palm and coconut oils have higher levels.
- Cholesterol in food is not the only factor; overall diet and lifestyle matter.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Water released
blocks.statement: How many water molecules are released when one triglyceride forms from glycerol and three fatty acids?
steps: Each ester bond forms with the loss of one water molecule.
There are three ester bonds, so three molecules of water.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Compare
blocks.statement: Why is groundnut oil liquid at room temperature while butter is solid?
steps: Groundnut oil has more unsaturated fatty acids (double bonds), which stop the chains packing tightly.
Butter has more saturated fatty acids, which pack closely and are solid.

objectives: Describe amino acids and the peptide bond

reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Limiting amino acids for cereals (lysine) and legumes (methionine) are standard textbook statements; confirm with the syllabus. Number of essential amino acids (9 for adults) is a common value.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Amino acids and peptides
blocks.md: An **amino acid** has an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH) and a side chain (R). Two amino acids join by a **peptide bond** (a condensation reaction releasing water) to make a **dipeptide**; a chain is a **polypeptide**. Joining n amino acids forms n - 1 peptide bonds. A protein is one or more folded polypeptides.

blocks.title: Essential amino acids and quality
blocks.md: Humans cannot make **nine essential amino acids** (for adults), so they must come from food. **High-quality (first-class) proteins** (eggs, milk, meat, fish) contain all of them in good proportions and are well digested. Many plant proteins are low in one or more (cereals are often low in lysine; legumes are often low in methionine); **protein complementation** (e.g. maize with beans) gives a better amino acid pattern.

items.text: Two amino acids join: peptide bond

blocks.caption: Two amino acids combining to form a dipeptide and a molecule of water.
blocks.alt: Diagram: amino acid 1 plus amino acid 2 gives a dipeptide plus water.

blocks.title: Nitrogen balance
blocks.md: Proteins contain nitrogen. **Positive nitrogen balance** (intake greater than loss) occurs in growth, pregnancy and recovery; **negative** balance in starvation, illness and inadequate protein. Protein supplies 17 kJ/g, but it is best saved for growth and repair by providing enough energy from carbohydrate and fat (the **protein-sparing** effect).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Essential does not mean 'most important'; it means the body cannot make it.
- 'Vegetarian protein is poor' is wrong if foods are combined well and the diet is varied.
- Severe protein-energy malnutrition needs medical care, not just food advice.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Peptide bonds
blocks.statement: A polypeptide has 120 amino acids in a single chain. How many peptide bonds does it contain?
steps: Each bond joins two neighbouring amino acids.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Complementation
blocks.statement: Maize is low in lysine and beans have more lysine but less methionine. Why is a meal of both better?
steps: Each food supplies the amino acid that the other lacks.
Together the amino acid pattern is closer to the body's needs.
